influence.definition: To have an effect on the character, development, or behavior of someone or something.
influence.grammar_rule: Direct transitive verb without preposition! Do NOT use 'on' after the verb 'influence'. However, the noun 'influence' DOES take 'on'.
influence.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'It influences me' (no prep) ➔ Noun: 'It has an influence ON me' (uses ON)
examples: Weather can strongly influence people's mood.
His speeches influenced millions of voters.
influence.common_mistake: ❌ It influences on my decision. ➔ ✅ It influences my decision. (OR: It has an influence on my decision.)

affect.definition: To produce a change or influence in someone or something.
affect.grammar_rule: Direct transitive verb! Do NOT add 'on'. (Note: The noun 'effect' takes 'on').
affect.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'Climate change affects wildlife' (no prep) ➔ Noun: 'It has an effect ON wildlife' (uses ON)
examples: The new tax laws will affect small business owners.
Lack of sleep negatively affects your health.
affect.common_mistake: ❌ Smoking affects on health. ➔ ✅ Smoking affects health. (OR: Smoking has an effect on health.)

impact.definition: To have a strong effect or influence on someone or something.
impact.grammar_rule: As a verb, 'impact' can take a direct object or 'on'. As a noun, it always takes 'on'.
impact.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'This policy impacts local business' ➔ Noun: 'This policy has an impact ON local business'
examples: Technology heavily impacts our daily routines.
The decision will impact on future generations.
impact.common_mistake: ❌ A negative impact for society. ➔ ✅ A negative impact on society.

answer.definition: To say, write, or do something as a reaction to a question, call, or letter.
answer.grammar_rule: Direct transitive verb! Do NOT add 'to' when answering a question/person. However, the noun 'answer' takes 'to'.
answer.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'I answered her question' (no prep) ➔ Noun: 'Here is the answer TO her question' (uses TO)
examples: Please answer the phone.
He answered all my questions patiently.
answer.common_mistake: ❌ She answered to my email. ➔ ✅ She answered my email. (OR: She sent an answer to my email.)

contact.definition: To communicate or get in touch with someone by phone, email, or letter.
contact.grammar_rule: Direct transitive verb without preposition. However, the phrase 'be in contact' takes 'with'.
contact.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'Contact me tomorrow' (no prep) ➔ Noun: 'Keep in contact WITH me' (uses WITH)
examples: Please contact customer support for assistance.
I will contact you as soon as I arrive.
contact.common_mistake: ❌ Contact with me later. ➔ ✅ Contact me later.

visit.definition: To go to see a person or place for pleasure, business, or social reasons.
visit.grammar_rule: Direct transitive verb! Do NOT use 'to'. However, the noun 'visit' takes 'to'.
visit.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'We visited Rome last summer' (no prep) ➔ Noun: 'We paid a visit TO Rome' (uses TO)
examples: We visited our grandparents last weekend.
Thousands of tourists visit the museum every day.
visit.common_mistake: ❌ I visited to London. ➔ ✅ I visited London. (OR: I went on a visit to London.)

approach.definition: To come near or nearer to someone or something in distance or time.
approach.grammar_rule: Direct transitive verb! Do NOT add 'to'. However, the noun 'approach' takes 'to'.
approach.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'The train approached the station' (no prep) ➔ Noun: 'Our approach TO the problem' (uses TO)
examples: As winter approaches, temperatures drop.
A stranger approached me on the street.
approach.common_mistake: ❌ He approached to the manager. ➔ ✅ He approached the manager.

lack.definition: To not have or not have enough of something.
lack.grammar_rule: As a verb, 'lack' takes a direct object (no preposition). As a noun, 'lack' takes 'of'.
lack.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'He lacks confidence' (no prep) ➔ Noun: 'A lack OF confidence' (uses OF)
examples: The applicant lacks relevant work experience.
She never lacks creative ideas.
lack.common_mistake: ❌ He lacks of experience. ➔ ✅ He lacks experience. (OR: He suffers from a lack of experience.)

demand.definition: To ask for something authoritatively or forcefully.
demand.grammar_rule: Verb takes a direct object without preposition. Noun 'demand' takes 'for'.
demand.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'They demand higher wages' (no prep) ➔ Noun: 'There is a high demand FOR workers' (uses FOR)
examples: Workers demand fair compensation.
The customer demanded an immediate refund.
demand.common_mistake: ❌ They demanded for an answer. ➔ ✅ They demanded an answer.

request.definition: To ask for something politely or formally.
request.grammar_rule: Direct transitive verb without preposition. Noun 'request' takes 'for'.
request.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'She requested assistance' (no prep) ➔ Noun: 'A request FOR assistance' (uses FOR)
examples: Passengers are requested to remain seated.
I requested a copy of the official transcript.
request.common_mistake: ❌ I requested for a room upgrade. ➔ ✅ I requested a room upgrade.

arrive.pattern: arrive at [building / station] OR arrive in [city / country]
arrive.grammar_rule: Use 'arrive AT' for buildings, stations, airports, events. Use 'arrive IN' for cities, countries, towns. NEVER use 'to'!
examples: We arrived at the airport two hours early.
They arrived in Tokyo yesterday evening.
arrive.common_mistake: ❌ We arrived to London. ➔ ✅ We arrived in London.

agree.pattern: agree with [person] / agree on [topic] / agree to [proposal]
agree.definition: To share the same opinion or accept a proposal.
agree.grammar_rule: Use 'with' for people, 'on/about' for topics/terms, and 'to' for plans/terms/requests.
examples: I completely agree with you.
They agreed on the price.
She agreed to our terms.
agree.common_mistake: ❌ I am agree with you. ➔ ✅ I agree with you.

ask.definition: To inquire about something or request an item/favor.
ask.grammar_rule: 'Ask someone' (direct object for question/person); 'ask FOR something' when requesting an item or help.
examples: Can I ask you a question?
If you need help, don't hesitate to ask for it.
She asked about your health.
ask.common_mistake: ❌ Ask to the teacher a question. ➔ ✅ Ask the teacher a question.

pay.definition: To give money for goods, services, or debts.
pay.grammar_rule: Direct object for the bill/money ('pay the bill'); use 'FOR' when specifying the item bought ('pay for the coffee').
examples: I will pay the bill.
How much did you pay for that jacket?
Pay attention to the details!
pay.common_mistake: ❌ Pay the coffee. ➔ ✅ Pay for the coffee.

believe.pattern: believe [someone / statement] (VT) / believe in [god / concept / oneself] (VI)
believe.definition: To accept something as true, or have faith/trust in something.
believe.grammar_rule: Transitive direct 'believe someone' = trust their words. Intransitive 'believe IN someone' = trust their character/existence.
examples: I believe every word she said.
Do you believe in magic?
Always believe in yourself.
believe.common_mistake: ❌ I believe in what you said. ➔ ✅ I believe what you said.

worry.definition: To feel anxious or uneasy about actual or potential problems.
worry.grammar_rule: Intransitive uses 'about'. Passive / state form: 'be worried ABOUT'.
examples: Don't worry about the future.
Parents always worry about their children.
worry.common_mistake: ❌ Don't worry for this. ➔ ✅ Don't worry about this.

laugh.definition: To make sounds and facial movements expressing amusement or ridicule.
laugh.grammar_rule: Requires 'at' when directed at a person, joke, or situation.
examples: Everyone laughed at his hilarious joke.
Don't laugh at other people's mistakes.
laugh.common_mistake: ❌ Don't laugh on him. ➔ ✅ Don't laugh at him.

look at.definition: To direct your eyes toward someone or something to see them.
look at.grammar_rule: Requires 'at' when specifying the target of sight.
examples: Look at that beautiful painting on the wall!
She looked at me and smiled.
look at.common_mistake: ❌ Look to the board! ➔ ✅ Look at the board!

look for.definition: To attempt to find someone or something that is lost or needed.
examples: I am looking for my car keys.
Are you looking for a new job?
look for.common_mistake: ❌ I am looking my keys. ➔ ✅ I am looking for my keys.

look after.definition: To take care of or be responsible for someone or something.
look after.grammar_rule: Inseparable phrasal verb. Equivalent to 'take care of'.
examples: Could you look after my cat while I am away?
Nurses look after hospital patients around the clock.
look after.common_mistake: ❌ Look after of the baby. ➔ ✅ Look after the baby.

take care of.definition: To protect, mind, or handle responsibility for someone or something.
examples: She takes care of her elderly parents.
Don't worry about the bill; I will take care of it.
take care of.common_mistake: ❌ Take care for him. ➔ ✅ Take care of him.

think of.definition: To produce an idea or hold an opinion about something.
think of.grammar_rule: 'Think OF' is used for opinions ('What do you think of X?') or spontaneous ideas ('I thought of a plan').
examples: What do you think of his new proposal?
I can't think of her name right now.
think of.common_mistake: ❌ What do you think about the movie? (when asking overall impression) ➔ ✅ What do you think of the movie?

think about.definition: To consider or reflect deeply on something over a period of time.
think about.grammar_rule: 'Think ABOUT' implies active mental consideration or deliberation.
examples: I need some time to think about your offer.
What are you thinking about so intently?
think about.common_mistake: ❌ I am thinking to buy a house. ➔ ✅ I am thinking about buying a house.

depend.definition: To be controlled, decided, or influenced by someone or something else.
depend.grammar_rule: Always requires the preposition 'on' (or formal 'upon') before a noun or gerund object.
examples: Our weekend plans depend on the weather.
Children depend on their parents for love and security.
depend.common_mistake: ❌ It depends of the situation. ➔ ✅ It depends on the situation.

apologize.definition: To express regret or say sorry for doing something wrong.
apologize.grammar_rule: Use 'to' before the person receiving the apology, and 'for' before the reason or gerund (-ing).
examples: He apologized to his colleagues for being late.
You should apologize for making that remark.
apologize.common_mistake: ❌ He apologized me. ➔ ✅ He apologized to me.

discuss.definition: To talk about something in detail with someone.
discuss.grammar_rule: Strictly transitive direct verb! Do NOT add 'about' after 'discuss'.
examples: We need to discuss the new budget in tomorrow's meeting.
They discussed the problem openly.
discuss.common_mistake: ❌ We discussed about the project. ➔ ✅ We discussed the project.

look forward to.definition: To feel excited or pleased about something that is going to happen.
look forward to.grammar_rule: Inseparable 3-part phrasal verb. 'To' is a preposition; always follow with a noun or gerund (-ing).
examples: I look forward to meeting you next week.
She is looking forward to her summer vacation.
look forward to.common_mistake: ❌ I look forward to meet you. ➔ ✅ I look forward to meeting you.

listen.definition: To pay attention to sound or give attention to someone speaking.
listen.grammar_rule: Requires 'to' when followed by an object. Without an object, 'listen' stands alone.
examples: I love listening to jazz music in the evening.
Please listen to the teacher carefully.

turn down.pattern: turn down [something] OR turn [something / pronoun] down
turn down.definition: To reject an offer or invitation, or to reduce the volume/heat.
turn down.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb! Noun objects can go before or after 'down', but pronoun objects MUST go in between (e.g. 'turn IT down').
examples: She turned down the job offer in Paris.
Please turn the music down before midnight.
They offered him a promotion, but he turned it down.
turn down.common_mistake: ❌ He turned down it. ➔ ✅ He turned it down.

give up.pattern: give up [habit/item] / give [it] up / give up (intransitive)
give up.definition: To stop doing or having something, or to stop trying.
give up.grammar_rule: Transitive direct when stopping a habit (separable: 'give it up'). Intransitive when quitting effort ('Never give up!').
examples: He gave up smoking after ten years.
Don't give up! You are so close to solving the puzzle.
It was hard, but she finally gave it up.
give up.common_mistake: ❌ He gave up it last year. ➔ ✅ He gave it up last year.

carry on.definition: To continue doing something without stopping.
carry on.grammar_rule: Inseparable phrasal verb. Followed by gerund (-ing) or 'with' + noun.
examples: Please carry on with your work while I am out.
Despite the rain, they carried on playing football.
carry on.common_mistake: ❌ Carry on to read the book. ➔ ✅ Carry on reading the book.

look up to.definition: To admire and respect someone greatly.
look up to.grammar_rule: Three-part inseparable phrasal verb. Particles 'up to' cannot be split.
examples: Young athletes look up to Olympic champions.
She has always looked up to her older sister.
look up to.common_mistake: ❌ She looks up her mentor to. ➔ ✅ She looks up to her mentor.

break down.definition: To stop functioning (machinery/vehicle) or lose emotional control.
break down.grammar_rule: Purely intransitive phrasal verb when referring to mechanical failure or emotional tears.
examples: Our car broke down on the motorway.
She broke down in tears when she heard the touching news.
break down.common_mistake: ❌ The engine broke down us. ➔ ✅ The engine broke down.

run out of.definition: To use up all of a supply of something so that there is none left.
run out of.grammar_rule: Three-part inseparable phrasal verb. Requires object after 'of'.
examples: We have run out of milk; could you buy some?
I ran out of time before completing the last test question.
run out of.common_mistake: ❌ We ran out time. ➔ ✅ We ran out of time.

take off.pattern: take off (plane/success - VI) / take off [clothing] (VT separable)
take off.definition: To leave the ground (aircraft), become successful, or remove clothing.
take off.grammar_rule: Intransitive for planes/success ('The plane took off'). Separable transitive for clothing ('take off your coat' / 'take it off').
examples: The flight took off on schedule.
Please take off your shoes before entering.
It was hot, so he took it off.
take off.common_mistake: ❌ Take off it. ➔ ✅ Take it off.

put off.definition: To delay or postpone an event, or discourage someone.
put off.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb. Nouns can go after or middle; pronouns MUST go in middle ('put it off').
examples: Never put off until tomorrow what you can do today.
They put off the meeting until next Monday.
Don't let one bad experience put you off.
put off.common_mistake: ❌ Don't put off it. ➔ ✅ Don't put it off.

bring up.definition: To raise a child or to introduce a topic into conversation.
bring up.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb. Pronoun object MUST split verb and particle ('bring it up').
examples: She was brought up by her grandparents in Scotland.
Why did you bring up that uncomfortable subject at dinner?
It's a delicate topic, so don't bring it up.
bring up.common_mistake: ❌ Don't bring up it now. ➔ ✅ Don't bring it up now.

get along with.definition: To have a harmonious, friendly relationship with someone.
get along with.grammar_rule: Three-part inseparable phrasal verb. Cannot split 'along with'.
examples: Do you get along with your new room-mate?
He gets along well with all his colleagues.
get along with.common_mistake: ❌ I get along my boss. ➔ ✅ I get along with my boss.

call off.definition: To cancel an event, match, or planned agreement.
call off.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb. Pronoun object must go in middle ('call it off').
examples: They had to call off the football match due to heavy fog.
The strike was called off after negotiations succeeded.
They couldn't agree, so they called it off.
call off.common_mistake: ❌ They called off it. ➔ ✅ They called it off.

come across.definition: To find or meet someone or something by chance.
come across.grammar_rule: Inseparable phrasal verb! Do not place the object between 'come' and 'across'.
examples: While cleaning the attic, I came across an old family album.
She came across an interesting article in the magazine.
come across.common_mistake: ❌ I came an old photo across. ➔ ✅ I came across an old photo.

figure out.definition: To understand or solve something after thinking about it.
figure out.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb! 'Figure it out' is the mandatory pronoun placement.
examples: It took me an hour to figure out how to assemble the desk.
Don't worry, we will figure it out together.
figure out.common_mistake: ❌ We must figure out it. ➔ ✅ We must figure it out.

fall out with.definition: To argue with someone and stop being friendly with them.
examples: He fell out with his best friend over a silly argument.
They haven't spoken since they fell out last year.
fall out with.common_mistake: ❌ She fell out her colleague. ➔ ✅ She fell out with her colleague.

set up.definition: To establish a business, organization, system, or equipment.
set up.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb. 'Set it up' requires pronoun in the middle.
examples: She set up her own graphic design agency in 2020.
The IT team will set up your laptop this afternoon.
Here is your new router; let's set it up.
set up.common_mistake: ❌ Set up it now. ➔ ✅ Set it up now.

work out.pattern: work out (exercise - VI) / work out [a plan] (VT separable)
work out.definition: To exercise physically (VI), or calculate/solve a problem (VT separable).
work out.grammar_rule: Intransitive for physical fitness. Separable transitive when solving/calculating ('work it out').
examples: I work out at the gym three times a week.
We need to work out a strategy before launching.
The math problem was tough, but he worked it out.
work out.common_mistake: ❌ Work out it carefully. ➔ ✅ Work it out carefully.

catch up with.definition: To reach the same level/position as someone, or meet up to share news.
examples: She ran fast to catch up with the lead runner.
Let's grab coffee this weekend to catch up with each other.
catch up with.common_mistake: ❌ Catch up my friends. ➔ ✅ Catch up with my friends.

keep up with.definition: To move at the same speed as someone, or stay informed about current events.
examples: Slow down! I can't keep up with you.
It is difficult to keep up with rapid technological changes.
keep up with.common_mistake: ❌ Keep up the technology trends. ➔ ✅ Keep up with technological trends.

examples: The room was so hot that two attendees passed out.
He nearly passed out from exhaustion.
pass out.common_mistake: ❌ He passed out the exam. ➔ ✅ He passed out (fainted).

look into.definition: To investigate, research, or examine a problem or situation.
look into.grammar_rule: Inseparable phrasal verb! Always put object after 'into'.
examples: The police are looking into the cause of the fire.
Our support team will look into your complaint immediately.
look into.common_mistake: ❌ I will look the complaint into. ➔ ✅ I will look into the complaint.

put up with.definition: To tolerate or endure an unpleasant person or situation without complaining.
examples: I don't know how she puts up with all that noise.
We shouldn't have to put up with rude behavior.
put up with.common_mistake: ❌ Put up the noise. ➔ ✅ Put up with the noise.

go through.definition: To experience a difficult situation, or examine details in documents.
examples: She has gone through a tough time recently.
Let's go through the contract step by step.
go through.common_mistake: ❌ Go the document through. ➔ ✅ Go through the document.

bring about.definition: To cause something to happen or exist.
bring about.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb. 'Bring it about' requires pronoun in middle.
examples: New policy changes brought about significant improvement.
What brought about this sudden decision?
bring about.common_mistake: ❌ Bring about it. ➔ ✅ Bring it about.

cut down on.definition: To reduce the amount or quantity of something consumed.
examples: The doctor advised him to cut down on sugar.
We need to cut down on monthly household expenses.
cut down on.common_mistake: ❌ Cut down sugar. ➔ ✅ Cut down on sugar.

get over.definition: To recover from an illness, shock, or emotional difficulty.
get over.grammar_rule: Inseparable phrasal verb! Object always follows 'over'.
examples: It took him weeks to get over the flu.
She finally got over her breakup.
get over.common_mistake: ❌ I got the cold over. ➔ ✅ I got over the cold.

grow up.pattern: grow up (in a place / as a child)
grow up.definition: To gradually advance from childhood to adulthood.
grow up.grammar_rule: Intransitive phrasal verb. (Compare with transitive 'bring up' = raise a child).
examples: He grew up in a small coastal town.
What do you want to be when you grow up?
grow up.common_mistake: ❌ She grew up her child. ➔ ✅ She raised / brought up her child.

show off.pattern: show off (boast - VI) / show off [skills] (VT separable)
show off.definition: To boast or display abilities/possessions proudly to impress others.
show off.grammar_rule: Intransitive when boasting ('Stop showing off!'). Separable transitive ('show off your trophy' / 'show it off').
examples: He loves showing off his sports car.
She bought a new jacket and couldn't wait to show it off.
show off.common_mistake: ❌ Show off it. ➔ ✅ Show it off.

pick up.definition: To lift something, collect a person/item, or learn a skill casually.
pick up.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb. 'Pick it up' requires pronoun in middle.
examples: He picked up the heavy box from the floor.
I will pick you up at the station at six.
She picked up conversational Italian while living in Rome.
pick up.common_mistake: ❌ Pick up it. ➔ ✅ Pick it up.

hold on.definition: To wait for a short time, or keep a tight grip on something.
examples: Hold on a minute, I need to tie my shoelace.
Hold on tight to the railing!
hold on.common_mistake: ❌ Hold on the phone me. ➔ ✅ Hold on a second.

back up.definition: To make a copy of computer files, or support a person/claim.
back up.grammar_rule: Separable phrasal verb. 'Back it up' requires pronoun in middle.
examples: Always back up your important documents to the cloud.
My colleagues backed me up during the board meeting.
back up.common_mistake: ❌ Back up it. ➔ ✅ Back it up.

drop out of.definition: To quit a course, school, or competition before completion.
examples: He dropped out of university to start his own software company.
Injuries forced two runners to drop out of the marathon.
drop out of.common_mistake: ❌ Dropped out the school. ➔ ✅ Dropped out of school.

turn up.pattern: turn up (arrive - VI) / turn up [volume/heat] (VT separable)
turn up.definition: To arrive or appear unexpectedly (VI), or increase volume/sound (VT separable).
turn up.grammar_rule: Intransitive for arrival ('He turned up late'). Separable transitive for volume ('turn it up').
examples: He turned up at the party without an invitation.
Could you turn up the radio? I love this song.
Turn it up!
turn up.common_mistake: ❌ Turn up it. ➔ ✅ Turn it up.

work with.definition: To collaborate or cooperate with a team or client on a specific project or objective.
work with.grammar_rule: Multi-preposition structure: work WITH + person/team/company ON + project/task. Note: FOR + noun/gerund expresses purpose, whereas TO + verb infinitive expresses intention.
work with.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'work with a team on a project' ➔ Noun: 'collaboration WITH someone ON something'
examples: He works closely with his team to execute marketing campaigns.
She works with small businesses on social media strategy.
work with.common_mistake: ❌ Work to a team for a project. ➔ ✅ Work with a team on a project.

report to.definition: To be directly responsible to a supervisor, or to provide an account of progress.
report to.grammar_rule: Report TO + person (line manager/supervisor); report ON + subject/progress.
report to.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'He reports to the head of marketing' ➔ Noun: 'Direct report TO the director'
examples: He reports to the head of marketing and works closely with his team.
The regional managers report directly to the CEO.
report to.common_mistake: ❌ He reports at the manager. ➔ ✅ He reports to the manager.

coordinate with.definition: To organize activities so that people or teams work together effectively.
coordinate with.grammar_rule: Coordinate WITH + person/department ON + task/schedule. Use FOR + noun/gerund when stating the target reason.
coordinate with.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'Coordinate with colleagues' ➔ Noun: 'Coordination WITH the team'
examples: She coordinates with her team to meet sales targets.
We need to coordinate with the logistics department on delivery dates.
coordinate with.common_mistake: ❌ Coordinate to the team. ➔ ✅ Coordinate with the team.

responsible for.definition: Having the duty to take care of someone or something, or being the cause of an outcome.
responsible for.grammar_rule: Adjective phrase requiring FOR + noun or gerund (-ing). Do NOT use TO + verb infinitive directly after 'responsible for'.
responsible for.noun_parallel: ⚡ Adjective: 'responsible FOR overseeing' ➔ Noun: 'take responsibility FOR something'
examples: Sarah is responsible for overseeing the entire organization.
Who is responsible for managing customer feedback?
responsible for.common_mistake: ❌ She is responsible to oversee the team. ➔ ✅ She is responsible for overseeing the team.

in charge of.definition: Having control of or responsibility for a department, team, or task.
in charge of.grammar_rule: Prepositional idiom requiring OF + noun or gerund (-ing). Use FOR when expressing purpose separately.
examples: She's in charge of setting the company's vision and goals.
Who is in charge of handling client contracts?
in charge of.common_mistake: ❌ In charge for setting goals. ➔ ✅ In charge of setting goals.

comply with.definition: To act in accordance with a wish, command, law, or rule.
comply with.grammar_rule: Inseparable verb + preposition structure. Always requires 'with'.
comply with.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'comply with safety regulations' ➔ Noun: 'in compliance WITH standards'
examples: All products must comply with international safety standards.
Failure to comply with the rules may result in penalties.
comply with.common_mistake: ❌ Comply to the regulations. ➔ ✅ Comply with the regulations.

specialize in.definition: To concentrate on and become an expert in a particular subject or skill.
specialize in.grammar_rule: Requires 'in' followed by a noun or gerund (-ing).
specialize in.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'specialize in corporate law' ➔ Noun: 'specialization IN marketing'
examples: Our firm specializes in environmental law and sustainability.
She specialized in pediatric medicine during residency.
specialize in.common_mistake: ❌ Specialize on international trade. ➔ ✅ Specialize in international trade.

succeed in.definition: To achieve the desired aim or result in a task or career.
succeed in.grammar_rule: Requires 'in' + gerund (-ing). Do NOT use TO + infinitive after 'succeed' when stating the action achieved.
succeed in.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'succeed in passing the exam' ➔ Noun: 'success IN business'
examples: She succeeded in securing funding for the new start-up.
If you work hard, you will succeed in achieving your goals.
succeed in.common_mistake: ❌ He succeeded to pass the test. ➔ ✅ He succeeded in passing the test.

attribute to.definition: To regard something as being caused by someone or something.
attribute to.grammar_rule: Complex structure: attribute SOMETHING (direct object) TO SOMETHING/SOMEONE (cause).
attribute to.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'attribute success to hard work' ➔ Noun: 'an attribution TO the author'
examples: The CEO attributed the rise in profits to strong teamwork.
Scientists attribute global warming to greenhouse gas emissions.
attribute to.common_mistake: ❌ He attributed the success for his team. ➔ ✅ He attributed the success to his team.

refrain from.definition: To stop oneself from doing something or acting on an impulse.
examples: Please refrain from smoking inside the auditorium.
Passengers are requested to refrain from using mobile phones during takeoff.
refrain from.common_mistake: ❌ Refrain to speak during the presentation. ➔ ✅ Refrain from speaking during the presentation.

apply.definition: To make a formal request for a job, position, visa, or program.
apply.grammar_rule: Apply FOR + position/thing requested; apply TO + company/institution/person receiving application.
apply.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'apply for a job to a company' ➔ Noun: 'an application FOR a job TO a company'
examples: She applied for a project manager position at Google.
I am applying to three universities in the UK.
apply.common_mistake: ❌ Apply a job to the company. ➔ ✅ Apply for a job at/to the company.

focus on.definition: To give central attention or effort to a particular topic or task.
focus on.grammar_rule: Always requires 'on' before a noun, pronoun, or gerund (-ing). Do NOT use 'in' or 'to'.
focus on.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'focus on key priorities' ➔ Noun: 'maintain focus ON priorities'
examples: Let's focus on solving the primary bottleneck first.
He needs to focus on improving his conversational skills.
focus on.common_mistake: ❌ Focus in the project. ➔ ✅ Focus on the project.

rely on.definition: To depend on or trust someone/something to work or act properly.
rely on.grammar_rule: Requires 'on'. Followed by noun, pronoun, or gerund (-ing).
rely on.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'rely on facts' ➔ Noun: 'place reliance ON data'
examples: You can always rely on her to deliver high-quality work on time.
Modern businesses rely heavily on cloud infrastructure.
rely on.common_mistake: ❌ Rely of public transport. ➔ ✅ Rely on public transport.

belong to.definition: To be owned by someone, or be a member of a group.
belong to.grammar_rule: Requires 'to' before the owner or club/organization.
examples: This laptop belongs to the IT department.
Does this notebook belong to you?
belong to.common_mistake: ❌ It belongs for me. ➔ ✅ It belongs to me.

deal with.definition: To take action to handle, resolve, or cope with a situation or person.
examples: Customer service representatives deal with complaints every day.
How do you deal with stress at work?
deal with.common_mistake: ❌ Deal about the issue. ➔ ✅ Deal with the issue.

suffer from.definition: To experience physical or mental pain, illness, or hardship.
suffer from.grammar_rule: Requires 'from' when specifying the medical condition or hardship.
examples: Many adults suffer from chronic sleep deprivation.
The business suffered from severe cash flow problems.
suffer from.common_mistake: ❌ Suffer of migraines. ➔ ✅ Suffer from migraines.

prevent from.definition: To stop something from happening or stop someone from doing an action.
examples: Bad weather prevented us from leaving the port.
Proper security controls prevent hackers from accessing customer data.
prevent from.common_mistake: ❌ Prevent him to enter the building. ➔ ✅ Prevent him from entering the building.

insist on.definition: To demand something forcefully and refuse to accept any refusal.
insist on.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'insist on paying' ➔ Noun: 'an insistence ON quality'
examples: He insisted on paying for everyone's dinner.
Why do you insist on doing everything by yourself?
insist on.common_mistake: ❌ Insist to pay the bill. ➔ ✅ Insist on paying the bill.

participate in.definition: To take part in an event, activity, or conversation.
participate in.grammar_rule: Requires 'in'. Followed by noun or gerund (-ing).
participate in.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'participate in workshops' ➔ Noun: 'participation IN discussions'
examples: All team members are encouraged to participate in weekly discussions.
Over fifty countries participated in the climate summit.
participate in.common_mistake: ❌ Participate at the meeting. ➔ ✅ Participate in the meeting.

benefit from.definition: To receive an advantage, profit, or help from something.
benefit from.grammar_rule: Verb 'benefit FROM' takes 'from'. Note: noun 'benefit OF' takes 'of'.
benefit from.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'benefit from training' ➔ Noun: 'the benefit OF experience'
examples: Students benefit from regular personalized feedback.
The local community will benefit greatly from the new sports center.
benefit from.common_mistake: ❌ Benefit of the new system. (when used as verb) ➔ ✅ Benefit from the new system.

approve of.definition: To think that someone or something is good, right, or acceptable.
approve of.grammar_rule: Intransitive + preposition 'of'. Transitive direct 'approve something' means officially sign/authorize.
approve of.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'approve of your choice' ➔ Noun: 'give approval OF/FOR a plan'
examples: Her parents didn't approve of her decision to leave university.
Do you approve of the new office policies?
approve of.common_mistake: ❌ I approve for your plan. ➔ ✅ I approve of your plan.

object to.definition: To express disagreement with or opposition to something.
object to.grammar_rule: Requires 'to' + noun or gerund (-ing). 'To' is a preposition here, NOT an infinitive marker.
object to.noun_parallel: ⚡ Verb: 'object to changing terms' ➔ Noun: 'raise an objection TO terms'
examples: Several residents object to building a highway near the school.
No one objected to the proposed timetable.
object to.common_mistake: ❌ I object to change the plan. ➔ ✅ I object to changing the plan.
